Apple has recently agreed to acquire a company called PlasmaSolve, according to a filing required by the European Union. Here's why this acquisition could be significant for Apple's future product roadmap.

The acquisition of PlasmaSolve could help Apple develop unique new product designs

Apple is famously secretive and rarely discloses its acquisitions unless required. However, as a designated "Gatekeeper" by the EU, Apple must publish details of several acquisitions, which are then posted on an EU website.

Here's what the latest filing says:

According to its website, PlasmaSolve was founded in 2016 by "experts in plasma propulsion technology and materials science." The company aims to "build reliable and accurate digital twins of these cutting-edge technologies by combining physics simulation, chemistry simulation, machine learning, data mining, and materials characterization techniques."

Why does Apple want to acquire this company?

In 2023, PlasmaSolve expanded its business to "develop highly specialized plasma simulation software called MatSight."

MatSight helps hardware manufacturers more effectively simulate how plasma processes perform—for instance, applying ultra-thin coatings to the surfaces of three-dimensional objects like iPhones. MatSight ensures the coating is evenly applied across different curved surfaces, buttons, and other locations.

Understandably, Apple hasn't revealed its specific plans for the company. But PlasmaSolve's technology seems well-suited to helping Apple experiment with more unique hardware designs, materials, and form factors.

Last year's iPhone Air kicked off a new wave of unique designs, and there are reportedly more on Apple's product roadmap. A foldable iPhone Ultra is expected this fall, and a new design is anticipated for the iPhone's twentieth anniversary next year. Apple Watch, MacBook, and other products are also reportedly set for major redesigns. Major redesigns often come with new materials, new shapes, new sizes, and other challenges.

Based on what's known so far about the company, PlasmaSolve could be one piece of the puzzle that makes it easier for Apple to apply plasma processes—such as ultra-thin coatings—to all sorts of new product designs.
